title: Reset your life in 30 days: 3 proven Harvard & Stanford frameworks for any age
summary: Jean and Cherie walk through three frameworks for starting over: William Bridges' Transitions (ending, neutral zone, new beginning), Carol Dweck's growth mindset, and Bill Burnett and Dave Evans' Designing Your Life. Using themselves as case studies (Jean leaving Snap after seven years and ending an eight-year relationship at 35, Cherie surviving a computer science major), they argue that you must sit in the neutral zone before rushing to a new beginning, that a growth mindset is a choice anyone can adopt, and that small prototype experiments beat endless pondering. Each framework comes with a short exercise.

ideas.idea: Change is external (like changing jobs) while transition is an internal process with three stages: ending, neutral zone and new beginning.
ideas.detail: From William Bridges' book 'Transitions'; Cherie says naming the stages matters because go-go-go people like her rush to the new beginning as a way to avoid processing hurt.

ideas.idea: The neutral zone feels slow and unproductive day to day, but journaling, gym and reflection compound over time and are what make a genuine new beginning possible.
ideas.detail: At 35 Jean left her head of product role at Snap after seven years and ended an eight-year relationship and engagement, losing her whole conception of her future; only by slowly working through the neutral zone did she arrive at her current new beginning of moving in with Cherie and starting a venture together.

ideas.idea: Steve Jobs' ouster from Apple, years in the creative wilderness, and triumphant return illustrate that the neutral zone can be the source of fresh ideas.
ideas.detail: The hosts map his story onto ending, neutral zone and new beginning.

ideas.idea: Transitions exercise: write down one area of life that is ending or has just ended, how you feel about it, and one possibility that could bloom if you fully embrace the neutral zone.
ideas.detail: The framework applies to career, romance, friendship and anything else.

ideas.idea: Growth mindset is not a personality type; saying 'I'm not a growth mindset person' contradicts the concept, because anyone with a fixed mindset can choose to adopt a growth mindset.
ideas.detail: Carol Dweck (Stanford) contrasts the fixed mindset ('I'm either good at it or not') with the growth mindset ('with effort and perseverance I can figure it out'); growth-minded people route around obstacles while fixed-minded people see each obstacle as proof something can't happen.

ideas.idea: Doing one very hard thing roots a growth mindset in your body so that every later challenge feels solvable.
ideas.detail: Cherie's grueling computer science major, with all-nighters and seeking every resource, was the hardest thing she has done and left her feeling she can do anything.

ideas.idea: Jean attributes her entire career to a growth mindset: throwing herself into jobs she was unqualified for and trusting her ability to learn fast.
ideas.detail: She joined Goldman barely knowing Excel, never became top-50 percent at it yet was a top-performing analyst; that gave her the courage to become a product manager knowing nothing about product management, and later to go on camera for the podcast and start a CPG matcha brand after a career in digital products.

ideas.idea: Working for yourself on something you believe in lets you give 120 percent with no regrets, which you would never do 'working for the man'.
ideas.detail: The sisters describe building the airplane while flying it with Sisters Matcha, knowing no one in the industry, and finding it both scary and the most fun year of their lives.

ideas.idea: Only partner with someone who has a growth mindset, because a couple must be able to grow and move in the same direction rather than 'this is who I am, don't try to change me'.
ideas.detail: Jean frames it as dating a 'default yes' or 'default maybe' person over a 'default no'; a date who happily came to a Broadway rave and had the time of his life was her example.

ideas.idea: Ask your partner 'How can I love you better?' as a daily mantra to root a relationship in growth.
ideas.detail: Cherie learned it from two recently married friends who both work and ask each other this after long days; she aspires to that intentionality.

ideas.idea: Growth mindset exercise: identify a limiting belief and rewrite it as a mantra, 'manifestation but better'.
ideas.detail: Stanford professor Joel Peterson believed he let his emotions control him and turned it into the mantra 'I am not my emotions'.

ideas.idea: Designing Your Life applies design thinking to life through four parts: curiosity, prototyping experiences, reframing problems and radical collaboration, favoring small experiments over endless pondering.
ideas.detail: From the Stanford class and book by Bill Burnett and Dave Evans; it cuts wasted time by letting you test ideas quickly.

ideas.idea: Prototype a career hypothesis by inventing a low-stakes internship for yourself instead of theorizing about it.
ideas.detail: After leaving Snap, Jean took an unpaid one-day-a-week stylist internship at the Albright Fashion Library in LA to test a 20-year-old question of whether she wanted to work in fashion or just enjoy it as a consumer; 20 percent of the job was rearranging a shoe closet, and it was one of the most fulfilling things she has done.

ideas.idea: Design thinking breaks paralysis: when stuck, run a small test, because with a growth mindset you learn something whether or not it succeeds.
ideas.detail: The hosts tie the frameworks together: reflect in the neutral zone, then test a new beginning with a mini experiment that gathers information from the external world.

ideas.idea: Life design exercise: pick an area you want to pivot and brainstorm two tiny experiments to test it, sharing them publicly for accountability.
ideas.detail: Experiments don't need to be massive; the hosts promise to read and respond to comments.
